name: The Door-in-the-Face Technique
statement: Ask for far too much first, get refused, then the real, smaller request suddenly seems reasonable.
statementAccent: then the real, smaller request suddenly seems reasonable
meaning: The door-in-the-face technique is a compliance tactic in which a persuader first makes a large request they expect to be refused, then follows it with a smaller, more reasonable request, the one they actually wanted, which the target is then more likely to accept than if it had been made alone. The name comes from the image of the first request having a door slammed in its face. It was named and demonstrated by Robert Cialdini and colleagues in a 1975 study: students first asked to volunteer as counsellors for juvenile delinquents two hours a week for two years, which nearly all refused, were then asked to chaperone delinquents on a single two-hour trip to the zoo, and agreed at about fifty percent, far above the roughly one in six who agreed when asked only the zoo request. The technique is the mirror image of the foot-in-the-door approach and a mainstay of sales, negotiation, and fundraising.
mechanism: The primary explanation is reciprocity of concessions. By retreating from a large request to a smaller one, the requester appears to make a concession, and the norm of reciprocity presses the target to reciprocate that concession by conceding in turn, that is, by agreeing to the smaller request; the original paper is titled a reciprocal concessions procedure. A second mechanism is perceptual contrast: after the extreme first request, the second seems modest and reasonable by comparison. Guilt and self-presentation may also contribute, since refusing the first request can leave people wishing to appear helpful or to relieve discomfort. For the technique to work well, the same person should make both requests with little or no delay, so the second clearly reads as a concession, and the requests generally work better for prosocial causes. The tactic is the reverse of the foot-in-the-door technique, which starts small and escalates, whereas door-in-the-face starts large and retreats.

examples.text: In Cialdini's 1975 study, students who first refused a two-year counselling commitment agreed at about fifty percent to a single zoo trip, far above the control rate.
Scaling down from a large request to a small one reads as a concession, and the target feels pressed to reciprocate by agreeing to the smaller ask.
Opening with an extreme demand makes a subsequent, more moderate position look reasonable by contrast, a common negotiation use of the tactic.

variants.name: Reciprocal concessions
variants.text: The primary mechanism, in which the requester's retreat to a smaller request is a concession that the target feels obliged to reciprocate by agreeing.

variants.name: Perceptual contrast
variants.text: The secondary mechanism by which the smaller request appears modest and reasonable next to the extreme first request.

whyItMatters: The door-in-the-face technique is a classic finding in the psychology of compliance, showing that an initial refusal can be engineered to increase acceptance of a follow-up request. It gives concrete form to Cialdini's account of reciprocity of concessions, extending the reciprocity norm from goods to bargaining moves, and it illustrates how perceptual contrast shapes what seems reasonable. Widely used in sales, negotiation, and fundraising, it underlies the common practice of opening with an extreme position to make a target offer look moderate.

working.text: make a large request you expect to be refused, one clearly bigger than what you actually want.
after the refusal, present the smaller request, which now reads as a concession on your part.
rely on reciprocity and contrast, which press the target to accept the smaller request more than if asked alone.

limits: The door-in-the-face effect works best under specific conditions: the same person should make both requests, with little or no delay between them, and the cause is generally more effective when prosocial. If the first request is so extreme as to seem absurd or insincere, the concession may not register and the tactic can fail. Reported figures vary across accounts, with the control rate for the classic study cited variously in the range of roughly thirteen to seventeen percent, and meta-analyses find the technique about as effective overall as the opposite foot-in-the-door approach, so neither is clearly superior. The effect can also backfire if the target perceives manipulation. So while the core phenomenon is well established, its size and reliability depend heavily on timing, sincerity, and framing.
misreadings: The technique is not merely asking for a lot and settling for less by chance; it depends on the retreat being perceived as a genuine concession that invokes reciprocity, which is why timing and the same requester matter. It is not the same as the foot-in-the-door technique but its opposite, starting large rather than small. And the first request must be large yet not absurd; an unbelievable opening can read as insincere and kill the effect, so treating any extreme demand as automatically boosting compliance misjudges a tactic that hinges on the concession seeming real.
origin: Named and demonstrated by Robert Cialdini and colleagues in their 1975 study of reciprocal concessions, in which a refused large request raised compliance with a smaller follow-up; the opposite of the foot-in-the-door technique.
